Creation of a College Liaison Special Committee
Effective starting spring 2027
The College Liaison Special Committee shall consist of ten senators, one from each college that elects Faculty Senators and one from the Library, who are referred to as the ‘Liaison’ from their unit to the Faculty Senate. If the Faculty Senate votes to approve creation of this Special Committee in fall 2026, senators from each college/Library will select one of their number to serve during the spring 2027 semester in the role of Liaison. Following senate elections in May 2027, senators from each college/Library will again select one of their number in August to serve during the 2027-2028 academic year in the role of Liaison. Liaisons may be re-elected but must be a current senator. The Senate President and FSEC will ask for volunteers to chair this committee on a one-year basis and identify a chair for vote by the Faculty Senate at its September meeting.

College Liaison Committee members are charged with ensuring that faculty in each college are informed of pertinent university-level matters and communicate senate- and college-level concerns in both directions. Liaisons attend all-college faculty meetings and will be given the opportunity to give a report on senate activities. The Liaison also attends meetings of the Faculty Senate in their role as a current senator.
Liaisons have two responsibilities in addition to attending college- and senate-level meetings. First, Liaisons provide a brief monthly update regarding senate/university-level matters to faculty in their college. Second, Liaisons represent their college on the College Liaison Committee. This committee meets at least once per semester to address issues requiring inter-college coordination. The College Liaison Committee is a Special Committee of the Faculty Senate, chaired by the Vice President of the Faculty Senate who serves as a non-voting member.

FSEC Proposal - Introduction Only - Bill #2026-2027-FSEC-02 - Changing deadlines for course withdrawals.
Kristy Snow, CELS Academic Advisor, presented her draft bill which has been favorably reviewed and advanced by FSEC.

It was noted that advisors are attuned to students’ frustration with early withdrawal deadlines because, in many instances, they have yet to glean a robust assessment of whether or not they can be successful in a course.
They are forced to make guesses about how they might perform and many withdraw too soon, in an abundance of caution, which often has grave consequences.
Because withdrawals can impact things like full-time status, housing and financial aid, graduation date, etc. students would benefit from a more complete snapshot of how they are doing before making such decisions.
There were a number of questions from the floor and, while most senators were supportive of the move to extend the "withdraw without extenuating circumstances" period, there was concern that changing the deadline from three to eleven weeks was a bit extreme.
Data was presented from peer institutions who all have later deadlines than URI.
Other concerns centered around possible increased demand for faculty signatures, whether or not deadlines for accelerated and summer/J-term courses will also be adjusted (the current proposal only addresses 3

regular semester-long courses), and what impacts later withdrawals might have on group work of fellow students and on IDEA completions for faculty.
Sen.
Buxton suggested that the bill proposers perhaps also consider expanding the deadlines and relaxing the requirements for taking courses Pass-Fail rather than for a letter grade.
Students could then still keep earning credits so impacts on full-time status, degree completion dates, financial aid, etc. are somewhat mitigated.
Advisor Snow noted the usefulness of the feedback and she hopes to address many of the concerns in the next draft of the bill. d.
FSEC Proposal - Introduction Only - By-Laws Amendment - Bill #2026-2027-FSEC-01: Transitioning Special Committees to Standing Committees.
Senate President Preisser presented the draft bill which will be reviewed by CBUM before the next senate meeting when it will return for a vote.
He explained that, in recent memory, the senate has created new permanent committees without a complete understanding of their long-term need, the durability of their charge and resources available to help them address it, and the most appropriate membership composition to ensure the committee’s enduring success.

The proposal calls for a three-year “trial period,” wherein a special committee is created (through senate action, but without requiring an amendment to the university manual or by-laws) that performs a self-assessment during its third year and makes recommendations to the senate about whether to continue as a special committee, disband, or convert to a permanent committee.
This new process would apply to joint and sub-committees as well as senate standing committees.
Feedback was generally positive and it was noted that once a permanent, standing committee makes its way into the university manual and/or by-laws, it becomes difficult and cumbersome to refine its mission, charge and membership.
The new process would provide time to adopt the best possible manual language for new committees and ensure that practical concerns which can only be understood by seeing a committee in action are addressed from the start. e.

University of Rhode Island Academic Program Review Guidelines rev6.6.25 RHODE OF ISL HOPE LAND 1892
SECTION 1. ABOUT THE ACADEMIC PROGRAM REVIEW 4

Introduction The Academic Program Review (APR) at the University of Rhode Island is a valuable opportunity for all academic departments/units to celebrate achievements, shape the future of their academic department/units (referred to as departments herein), and ensure lasting impact for students, faculty, and the broader institution and community.
Through a systematic and structured process, APR engages faculty and staff in retrospective reflection and prospective planning to showcase program impact in ways that have shaped institutional priorities and investments with contributions to teaching, learning, research, scholarship, and student success, and to identify opportunities for growth and innovation.
APR fosters meaningful collaboration that is necessary to develop a shared vision and chart an inspiring course forward.
The Program Review Process and Report Development The program review process consists of several essential components, each playing a vital role in shaping the final report: 1.
Orientation: The APR journey begins with an orientation session designed to introduce faculty to the support structures available to them throughout their report writing effort.

At this first session, hosted by the Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and outcomes Assessment (JCAPROA), departments will also receive a preliminary program data packet provided by the Office of Institutional Research. 2.
Self-Study: Departments are asked to prepare a detailed Self-Study that examines how their activities in several areas (teaching, outcomes assessment, research, service and resource utilization, etc.) are aligned with the University’s Mission and Strategic Plan. (See Self Study Guidelines, Section 2) 3.
External Review: Departments are asked to invite a peer reviewer from a similar or aspirational department at another institution to provide an external perspective on the program’s strengths and identified growth areas.
The external reviewer’s report will include recommendations for improvement which should be integrated into the department’s Action Plan response. (See External Review, Section 3) 4.
Action Plan (Response and Strategic Planning): The Department Chair and Dean meet to discuss the external reviewer’s feedback, set response actions, 5

and develop a strategic Action Plan for the next six years. (See Action Plan, Section 4) Oversight and Support In addition to ongoing support available through the Office of the Provost, there are two key resources available to support departments throughout the APR process: ● Faculty Senate Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (JCAPROA) is responsible for overseeing, guiding and supporting the academic program review process, coordinating the scheduling of program reviews and maintaining the guidelines for reporting (University Manual 8.85.14) ● Office of Institutional Research disseminates university-level data and supports the departments with the interpretation of data.
Level of Organizational Evaluation URI Academic Program Review is at the department or academic program degree level, and at the college level for colleges without departments or with departments having fully integrated academic degrees.

For clarity within this document, the terms “department” or “unit” are used instead of “academic program.” Guidance for Specialized Accredited Units The APR process for units with specialized accreditation will be coordinated to avoid a duplication of effort.
These departments may also be reviewed independently of others within their academic unit.
Units with a combination of accredited and non- accredited programs are only required to address those areas not covered within their accreditation report within their Self-Study.
The Dean and Provost should receive both the accreditation report and the Self-Study when the APR report is submitted on behalf of the unit.
The proposed Action Plan should cover all programs within the unit (reference Action Plan, Section 4).
APR Review Cycle Departments are notified of an upcoming Academic Program Review reporting expectation the two semesters before the APR is due (e.g., notification in Fall of 2026 for APR due in Spring 2027).
The review cycle is intended to be every six years, with approximately 1/6 of the academic units reviewed each year.
Typically, all or most departments within a college are reviewed simultaneously.
The master schedule and timeline will be maintained by JCAPROA and available on the Provost’s Brightspace page. 6

Deferring Academic Program Review A one-year, one-time extension can be requested, with prior agreement from the Dean’s Office, by emailing the Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives and the Chair of JCAPROA (See Appendix A: Extension Request Form). Reasons for extensions can include, but are not limited to: leadership transitions, major curriculum changes, specialized accreditation review, institutional or strategic priorities, data availability and institutional changes, faculty workload and capacity, significant external changes (mergers, reorganizations, or new programs). Extensions beyond one-year will be considered on a case by case basis. Submission of the APR Departments should work in conjunction with their Dean’s Office to determine the method (e.g., email) and format (.pdf, word, etc.) the Dean prefers in order to receive and review the draft report. The Department Chair should upload the final APR report package to the Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives. 7

SECTION 2. THE SELF-STUDY 10

The Self-Study Academic Program Review includes a self-reflection on research and scholarly activities, teaching and curriculum development activities, public engagement activities and resource utilization.
The self-study is both a retrospective and a prospective activity which summarizes the current state of a department, analyzes trends since the last program review (when applicable), compares the academic program’s activities with benchmark data of similar academic programs (provided by URI’s Office of Institutional Research), and outlines an assessment process for continuous quality improvement of these programs and activities.
This retrospective analysis allows departments to explain how their past activities support their program’s strategic plan, the University’s mission and the curricular/academic plan.
Using data provided through the university data (e.g., data provided by Institutional Research and Enrollment Management), Hanover Data Reports, and internal department data collection over the past six years, programs examine progress on their performance goals and benchmarks.

The self-study will also present a plan for the future that includes ways to ensure improvement in the quality of academic programs and their services to the college, university, and community.
This prospective analysis allows academic programs to articulate response strategies to the opportunities and challenges within their discipline, university and higher education, and to establish forward-looking goals and benchmarks to be pursued during the next planning cycle.
The audience for the self-study includes the Dean, Provost, Vice Provost, the external reviewer(s) (see External Review, Section 3), and the faculty, staff, and administrators within the college.
Guidelines for Completion of the Self-Study Report: 1.
The 20-30 page report (plus appendices) should be an honest evaluation, providing feasible mechanisms for advancing quality. 2.
The report should be comprehensive yet succinct, focusing on key issues, with each section being descriptive and evaluative. 3.
The report should reflect the views of the faculty for the department/unit under review. 4.
Two main criteria should structure the review: Quality/Effectiveness and Efficiency. 11

a. Program quality/effectiveness addresses how well the Department does what it sets out to do. For example, how do the goals and objectives of the Department in terms of teaching, research, and public engagement compare to other benchmark programs, and how well are these achieved? Does it effectively serve the mission and strategic goals of the University? Is the Department innovative and of high quality? b. Program efficiency addresses the cost effectiveness of offerings of the Department. For example, what are the costs associated with its teaching, research, and public engagement activities? How effective is the Department in generating resources through attracting students, teaching and generating external funding in comparison to the level of institutional investment? Is it productive? Does it use its resources efficiently? c. SEE APPENDIX B FOR A TABLE OF DATA THAT DEPARTMENTS WILL USE TO INFORM THE SELF-STUDY 12

SECTION 3. THE EXTERNAL REVIEW 29

The External Review Process The external review (ER) process is designed to provide an outside perspective on the program’s strengths and areas for improvement.
The review is conducted by a peer from a similar program at another institution and results in a formal summary report.
Guidelines for the External Review Process: 1.
The unit lead identifies qualified individuals from peer institutions, ensuring any potential conflicts of interest are addressed early in the process. 2.
The department chair and Dean discuss possible external reviewers with the Dean.
External reviewers are chosen with the concurrence of the Dean. 3.
It is recommended that invitations to reviewers be sent by the department chair or Dean no less than eight months in advance of the scheduled site visit.
Chairs and Deans should determine who will send the email invitation. 4.
The External Reviewer discusses expected outcomes with the unit lead and sets a schedule for the site visit.
The unit lead prepares and provides a draft itinerary for the campus visit. 5.
The unit lead provides the External Reviewer with access to key documents, including the Self-Study, data reports, and strategic plans. 6.

During the site visit, the External Reviewer meets with faculty, students, and key stakeholders to assess the program.
Following the visit, the reviewer submits a formal written report with evaluative findings and recommendations, which are incorporated into the department’s action plan response.
Stakeholder meetings should be conducted without the chair present. 7.
The department and dean meet to discuss the reviewer’s findings and develop a formal response, including an action plan to address areas for improvement. 8.
The Provost’s Office will support a $1250 stipend plus travel expenses for one External Reviewer.
Colleges and departments can opt to contribute additional funds to support a larger stipend or to bring a second reviewer to campus.
Qualifications of External Reviewers 1.
Reviewer is from a comparable R1 program in quality, size and ranking. 2.
Reviewer has an arm’s length relationship with the URI program. 3.
Emeriti faculty from other universities who retired within the past year can be reviewers.
Providing context about how this person provides a visionary approach to the APR is helpful. 4.
Reviewers’ curriculum vitae should be shared with the dean before an invitation is extended to the prospective reviewer. 30

External Reviewer Report Guidelines The External Report (ER) is submitted by the external consultants to the Dean/Chair within three weeks of the site visit. The report should address the following: ● Executive Summary ● Introduction of reviewers and their roles ● Dates of the visit ● Consultant’s summary of strengths and challenges as identified in the Self-Study Report ● Consultant’s summary of strengths and challenges observed during the visit and not identified in the Self-Study Report ● Recommendations for how the department can expand on its strengths and address its challenges ● Additional information reviewer(s) deem relevant to address departmental goals 37

Requesting Funds for External Reviewers Note: Booking travel may be done by the reviewer themselves where they also pay themselves or by the department. Either way reimbursement will be made. The Provost Office will cover a $1,250 honorarium/stipend for up to two reviewers, as well as travel expenses (airfare, hotel, per diem, parking). However, we do not cover any meals with faculty members. If faculty are paying out of pocket for shared meals, then that would need to be reimbursed out of other department funds (this is not covered by the Provost’s Office). An expense breakdown should be included with a request for funding. If you are using department funds for the travel authorizations (TA's) then this expense breakdown is used as backup. The department gives an estimate of total expenses with complete information prior to the visit.
